L17: # Two-Weight Counterexamples to Devriendt's Resistance-Capacity Conjectures 7.6 and 7.7: Infinite Families, Sharp Minimal Witnesses, and an Unbounded Kron Obstruction Hierarchy
L18: This research presents explicit counterexamples to Conjectures 7.6 and 7.7 in Karel Devriendt’s “Graphs with Nonnegative Resistance Curvature,” Annals of Combinatorics 30 (2026), 415–438, published online in 2025, DOI: 【4†https://doi.org/10.1007/s00026-025-00774-x†doi.org】.
L19: It develops infinite families with positive integer conductances, retains sharp minimum-size counterexamples, and establishes a further obstruction theorem: networks of arbitrarily large order can fail capacity submodularity while every proper Kron reduction satisfies it.
L20: Zenodo: 【5†Two-Weight Counterexamples to Devriendt's Resistance-Capacity Conjectures 7.6 and 7.7: Infinite Families, Sharp Minimal Witnesses, and an Unbounded Kron Obstruction Hierarchy | Zenodo†zenodo.org】
L21: 
L22: The central question concerns the relationship between effective-resistance curvature and submodularity of resistance capacity. For a finite connected graph with positive edge conductances cᵢⱼ and effective resistances Rᵢⱼ, vertex resistance curvature is
L23: 
L24: pᵢ = 1 − ½∑ⱼ cᵢⱼRᵢⱼ.
L25: Writing r(U) = (1ᵀR[U]⁻¹1)⁻¹ for subsets containing at least two vertices, with singleton radius zero, normalized resistance capacity is τ(∅) = 0 and
L26: 
L27: τ(U) = ½ + r(U)/(2r(V))
L28: 
L29: for nonempty U. Submodularity requires every elementary gap
L30: 
L31: Δ(S;i,j) = τ(S∪{i}) + τ(S∪{j}) − τ(S) − τ(S∪{i,j})
L32: 
L33: to be nonnegative.
L34: Nonnegative resistance curvature is an established sufficient condition for submodular capacity. Conjecture 7.6 proposed the converse at the same weighting. Conjecture 7.7 proposed a graph-level characterization: a graph should admit a positive weighting with submodular capacity precisely when it admits a positive weighting with nonnegative curvature everywhere. The manuscript supplies separate counterexamples addressing these two quantifiers.
L35: For Conjecture 7.6, the construction works on every complete graph Kₙ with n ≥ 4. Choose one distinguished hub, assign conductance 2n−3 to its incident edges, and assign conductance 2n−7 to all remaining edges. Every elementary submodularity gap is strictly positive, although the hub has negative resistance curvature.
L36: 
L37: With m = n−1 and Dₘ = 2m²−3m−1, the curvature values are
L38: 
L39: p_hub = −1/Dₘ,
L40: p_outer = (2m−3)/Dₘ.
L41: The smallest complete-graph member has four vertices, spoke conductance 5, outer-edge conductance 1, curvature vector (−1/8, 3/8, 3/8, 3/8), and minimum elementary gap 5/1134. Thus the failure occurs even when every elementary inequality has a positive margin. Strictness also gives an open neighborhood under independent perturbations of the conductances at each fixed order.
L42: The proof establishes an exact boundary for the entire symmetric family. Let Cₘ(t) have one hub, m outer vertices, spoke conductance t > 0, and outer-edge conductance 1. Its capacity is submodular if and only if
L43: 
L44: Fₘ(t) = 4(t+m−1)(t+m) − m(m−1)(t+1)² ≥ 0.
L45: All elementary gaps are strictly positive exactly when Fₘ(t) > 0. Symmetry reduces the subset capacities to two formulas and the inequalities to five classes. Only the mixed hub–outer class can fail, and its binding case gives this single quadratic inequality. Substituting t = (2m−1)/(2m−5) proves the complete integer-weight family in every order.
L46: For Conjecture 7.7, the construction uses the split graph Gₖ = Kₖ ∨ Iₖ₊₁ for every k ≥ 2: a clique of k hubs joined to k+1 mutually nonadjacent outer vertices. Give hub–hub edges conductance 1 and hub–outer edges conductance k(k−1). Capacity is submodular, while
L47: 
L48: p_hub = −(k−1)/(2k³),
L49: p_outer = (2k−1)/(2k²).
L50: 
L51: Consequently, these examples have exactly k negatively curved vertices on 2k+1 vertices, giving an unbounded number of negative-curvature vertices.
L52: The stronger graph-level conclusion requires ruling out every alternative positive weighting on the same support. This is proved through spanning trees. If H is the hub set and e_H(T) counts hub–hub edges in a spanning tree T, then every spanning tree satisfies
L53: 
L54: ∑ₕ∈H deg_T(h) = 2k + e_H(T).
L55: 
L56: For the conductance-weighted spanning-tree distribution, the standard curvature identity therefore gives
L57: 
L58: ∑ₕ∈H pₕ = −½ E[e_H(T)] < 0.
L59: The inequality holds for every positive weighting. Hence this support can never have nonnegative curvature at every vertex, although the displayed weighting has submodular capacity. This establishes the graph-level failure independently of merely observing negative curvature in one example.
L60: A third result establishes minimal Kron obstructions of unbounded order. Kron reduction eliminates internal vertices by taking a Schur complement of the Laplacian while preserving effective resistances between retained vertices. For every m ≥ 3, consider Kₘ₊₂ with one hub, spoke conductance 2m−1, and outer-edge conductance 2m−5. Its full capacity is not submodular, yet every proper Kron reduction onto at least two vertices is submodular.
L61: Every proper reduction retaining at least three vertices has strictly positive elementary gaps; normalized two-vertex capacity has an unavoidable equality.
L62: The proof uses the same scalar boundary. Eliminating outer vertices preserves the spoke-to-outer conductance ratio up to common scaling, whereas eliminating the hub produces a uniform complete graph. At the chosen ratio, Fₘ(t) > 0 but Fₘ₊₁(t) < 0. Thus all proper reductions pass while the full network fails. The smallest example is a five-vertex complete graph with spoke conductance 5 and outer-edge conductance 1; its four negative full-scale gaps each equal −5/192.
L63: It follows that no fixed retained-vertex bound can certify capacity submodularity by checking all Kron reductions up to that size on graphs of unrestricted order.
L64: 
L65: The proofs are organized by an exact signed-curvature transport law. If T is retained and I is eliminated, then
L66: 
L67: p^(T) = p_T − L_TI L_II⁻¹p_I,
L68: 
L69: and the radius loss is
L70: 
L71: r(V) − r(T) = 2p_IᵀL_II⁻¹p_I.
L72: These identities connect elimination, curvature redistribution, and capacity gaps. They yield a pairwise quadratic criterion explaining how opposite-sign reduced curvatures can still satisfy submodularity. Classical resistance geometry, Schur complements, and spanning-tree identities provide the underlying tools.
L73: The release also retains sharp minimality results: fixed-weight counterexamples require at least four vertices and five edges, while graph-level counterexamples require at least five vertices and seven edges. The five-vertex graph-level support is unique up to isomorphism. Supplementary results include exact parameter intervals, support-relative perturbation neighborhoods, and an explicit robustness box for a four-vertex example.
L74: The significance is structural. The results establish that capacity submodularity is strictly weaker than nonnegative resistance curvature, both at a fixed weighting and at the level of which supports admit suitable weightings. They show that this separation persists through explicit infinite families and that arbitrarily large failures can remain invisible in every proper Kron reduction.
L75: The constructions and scalar criterion provide exact reference examples for further work in resistance geometry, discrete curvature, network reduction, and submodular set functions.
L76: The reproducibility package contains a six-page main manuscript, detailed proof supplements, verification source code, exact certificates, and 949 structured records across eight dataset configurations. Seventeen source verification programs passed. A separate exact data derivation reconstructs 19 finite graphs and recomputes 72,736 elementary gaps using rational arithmetic. Written arguments establish the infinite families; finite computations check the examples and identities.
L77: Research version: 3.0.0. All stated proof obligations have written arguments within the declared scope, and the supplied internal exact checks pass. Independent human review, proof-assistant certification, and historical priority remain unestablished. The number of negative vertices is unbounded, while their individual negative magnitudes decrease with order. Perturbation robustness is asserted at each fixed order.
L78: The Kron hierarchy establishes a limitation of bounded-retained-order testing, without claiming a general computational-hardness theorem.

Every graphic matroid is SIBO.
By case (v) above, Conjecture 1.3 would imply Conjecture 1.1 for graphic matroids. Let
us note that Conjecture 1.3 is a strengthening of the graphic matroid case of the following
celebrated conjecture.
▶Conjecture 1.4 (Gabow [15], see also [48, 10]). Let A and B be bases of a rank-r matroid M.
Then, there are orderings a1, . . . , ar of A and b1, . . . , br of B such that {a1, . . . , ai, bi+1, . . . , br}
and {b1, . . . , bi, ai+1, . . . , ar} are bases for any i = 1, . . . , r.
In contrast to Conjecture 1.3, Conjecture 1.4 is known to hold for graphic matroids [48,
26, 10], regular matroids [4], and sparse paving matroids [5], which are the focus of this paper.
A rank-r matroid is paving if every circuit is of size either r or r + 1, and is sparse paving if
it and its dual are both paving. It is believed that asymptotically almost all matroids are
sparse paving, formally stated as follows.
▶Conjecture 1.5 (Mayhew, Newman, Welsh, and Whittle [34]). Let Mu(n) and Su(n) be the
families of all matroids and sparse paving matroids, respectively, on an unlabeled n-element
ground set. Similarly, let Ml(n) and Sl(n) be their counterparts on a labeled n-element
ground set. Then,
lim

holds.
Under Conjecture 1.5, the result of [5] implies that Conjecture 1.4 holds asymptotically.
